extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers and creative-writing students interested in using unreliable narrators
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for creating and evaluating unreliable narrators in fiction, including types, craft techniques, quality criteria, and common failure modes. Focused on how to make unreliability purposeful, discoverable, and satisfying for readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Deliberate Liar
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrator who consciously misleads readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used when the narrator intentionally deceives; examples include Humbert Humbert (Lolita) and the narrator of Gillian Flynn's Gone Girl. Useful to create dramatic irony and moral complexity, but must be motivated by character.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Self‑Deceiver
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrator who believes their own false narrative; narrating in good faith but deluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creates tragic or sympathetic unreliability (example: Stevens in The Remains of the Day). The unreliability should arise from the narrator's psychology, not authorial manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Mentally Compromised
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrator whose perception is affected by illness, trauma, or substances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Christopher in The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night‑Time; the narrator in Memento. Use carefully to avoid clichés or exploitative portrayals; details may be distorted by cognitive or sensory limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Naïve Observer
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrator who lacks experience or knowledge to understand events (children, sheltered narrators).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Scout in To Kill a Mockingbird, Holden Caulfield. The gap between perception and reality creates dramatic irony; the narrator's limited vocabulary/insight should be consistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Morally Ambiguous
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrator whose values skew their interpretation of events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Patrick Bateman (American Psycho), the narrator of A Clockwork Orange. Moral distortion can generate dark humor or horror; the reader must be able to infer the ethical gap.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Unwitting (Plot‑Level)
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrator who does not know key facts that the reader or other characters do (asymmetric information).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This creates suspense and dramatic irony; ensure the information imbalance is plausible and not a contrivance.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Ironic / Implied‑Author Distant
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrator whose worldview is distinct from the implied author's, allowing readers to see through the narrator's perspective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The implied author provides ironic distance; signals must exist so the reader can judge the narrator against the implied author's standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish trust first
rubrics_metrics.description: Settle readers into believing the narrator early on so the later reveal feels consequential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build rapport through plausibility and consistent detail; if the narrator never seems credible, the revelation won't land.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plant subtle inconsistencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Embed small contradictions that are easy to miss on first read but become clear in hindsight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make inconsistencies subtle and character‑consistent so re‑reading rewards the reader; avoid obvious contradictions that prematurely break suspension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mostly accurate details
rubrics_metrics.description: Use mostly accurate or verifiable details; outright lies from the start break trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True or concrete specifics anchor the narrator; lying about everything undermines the device and alienates readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivated unreliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Unreliability must have an internal reason rooted in character or plot, not just serve plot mechanics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide psychological, social, or situational motives for deception or misperception so the device feels organic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic reveal
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether the unreliability is revealed in a dramatic single moment, gradually, or never fully confirmed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each approach has different effects: a single reveal can be shocking, gradual revelation builds slow dread/insight, and ambiguity preserves tension—choose based on thematic goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ironic distance
rubrics_metrics.description: Let the implied author signal what the narrator misses so readers can perceive the gap.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tonal cues, contrast, or other characters' perspectives to create authorial irony without undercutting the narrator's voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purposeful unreliability
rubrics_metrics.description: The unreliability should be purposeful, not merely a gimmick.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It should serve theme, character development, or meaning rather than being used only for surprise or twist value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery deepens meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: The reader's discovery that the narrator is unreliable should deepen the work's meaning rather than merely surprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reveals should illuminate character, theme, or subtext; if they only produce shock, they feel cheap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re‑reading rewards
rubrics_metrics.description: A well-crafted unreliable narration rewards re‑reading with new perspective and layered understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design clues and structural echoes so subsequent reads reveal patterns and ironies missed initially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistent internal logic of narrator's voice
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrator's voice must be consistent within their own logic, even when mistaken or deceptive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain believable attitudes, knowledge limits, and linguistic patterns so the narrator's unreliability feels authentic rather than arbitrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author–reader knowing relationship
rubrics_metrics.description: The author and reader should maintain a knowing relationship behind the narrator's back.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signal to readers what the narrator misses; this shared knowledge produces dramatic irony and aligns reader sympathy or critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrator lies only for plot mechanics (failure mode)
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrator simply lies to make the plot work without believable character logic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti‑pattern: avoid manufactured lies that aren't motivated by the narrator's psychology; such cheats frustrate readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reveal erases everything before (failure mode)
rubrics_metrics.description: A reveal that retroactively invalidates prior events, making the earlier narrative meaningless (cheating).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti‑pattern: ensure earlier events retain meaning after the reveal; don't nullify stakes or emotional investment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inconsistencies are author errors, not character traits (failure mode)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent contradictions that are actually mistakes in writing rather than deliberate character‑based unreliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorally check that contradictions are purposeful; accidental inconsistencies break trust and harm craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader can never tell if anything is true (unmoored ambiguity) (failure mode)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ambiguity so extreme that readers cannot anchor themselves in any verifiable reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti‑pattern: provide enough anchors or signals so readers can make informed inferences; total unmooring frustrates rather than intrigues.

rubrics_metrics.name: "It was all a dream" cliché (failure mode)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a dream or similar device as the reveal, which feels clichéd and unsatisfying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid this shortcut; it typically negates stakes and betrays reader investment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Booth's distinction between reliable and unreliable narrators
rubrics_metrics.description: Reliable narrator: speaks/acts in accord with the norms of the work. Unreliable narrator: does not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the implied author as the standard against which to judge reliability; the implied author's norms determine when a narrator is unreliable.
